title: Does a 9 mg/dL difference matter to a patient?

objectives.statement: State what the phrase statistically significant claims about a result and what it leaves untouched, and repair a sentence that has slid from that technical sense into the everyday sense of the word.

Show that whether a difference reaches statistical significance depends on the size of the study as well as the size of the difference, so that a difference of no consequence can clear the conventional cut-off while a large difference misses it.

Distinguish an anchor-based or distribution-based estimate of a minimal clinically important difference from patient preference elicitation and from a prospectively justified service decision threshold, and explain what each can and cannot establish.

Place an effect estimate and its confidence interval against a stated importance threshold, classify the result into one of five positions, and state in the decision's own units what each position supports.
Judge a reported difference on magnitude, uncertainty, bias and real-world relevance together, and say plainly what the study does and does not license for the decision in front of you.

scenes.title: Somebody has to choose the number
Where the interval sits when a line is drawn
Practice: three passes at the same skill
Transfer: a different kind of number
Show that the two senses stay apart
Clinical wrap-up: the meeting where the block ends
